# Joining and Reshaping {#sec-joins}

A join has two failure modes, and neither raises an error. It can
drop rows, when a key present on one side is absent on the other,
and the analysis then proceeds on a smaller, and possibly
different, cohort than the one the methods section describes. Or
it can multiply rows, when a key that should be unique is not,
and a patient then contributes several times to an estimate that
assumed one contribution. The first shrinks the denominator; the
second corrupts the standard errors; both produce a data frame
that looks exactly like the one you wanted. What catches them is
not care but arithmetic: a stated expectation about how many rows
the result should have, checked against how many it does.

```

\end{flushright}
```
:::

## Choosing a join {#sec-joins-choosing}

Almost every biostatistical project joins tables: demographics to
outcomes, labs to medications, clinical data to imaging indices.
The operation is one function call, which is why the difficulty
never lives in the call. It lives in the question the join is
meant to answer, and in what the keys actually contain. The
generic tour of the two-table verbs is in R for Data Science
[@wickham2023r4ds, ch. 19]; this chapter keeps to the judgments a
clinical dataset forces on you.

### The `_join` family

`dplyr`'s two-table verbs:

| Function       | Returns                                            |
|----------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| `inner_join`   | Rows with a match in both                          |
| `left_join`    | All rows from `x`, NA in `y` columns where no match |
| `right_join`   | All rows from `y`, NA in `x` columns where no match |
| `full_join`    | All rows from both, NA in non-matching columns      |
| `semi_join`    | Rows of `x` with a match in `y` (no `y` cols)       |
| `anti_join`    | Rows of `x` with no match in `y`                    |

`semi_join` and `anti_join` are filtering joins: they filter `x`
based on `y` without adding `y`'s columns. The other four are
mutating joins: they add columns.[^pandas] The choice among the
mutating joins reduces to two questions, shown in
@fig-join-choice: do you want to keep rows that fail to match, and
if so, from which side.

[^pandas]: In `pandas`, the four mutating joins are one call,
    `x.merge(y, on="id", how=...)` with `how` set to `"inner"`,
    `"left"`, `"right"`, or `"outer"`. The filtering joins have no
    `merge` equivalent and are written with `isin()`, for example
    `x[~x["id"].isin(y["id"])]` for an anti-join.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-join-choice
%%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart for choosing a join. The first
%%|   question asks whether to keep rows with no match: no gives
%%|   inner_join. Yes leads to a second question asking which side
%%|   the unmatched rows come from: left x gives left_join, right y
%%|   gives right_join, and both gives full_join."
%%| fig-cap: "Choosing a join. The first question is whether unmatched
%%|   rows should survive; the second is from which table. The
%%|   filtering joins (semi, anti) answer a different question again:
%%|   keep or drop rows of x by their presence in y, adding no columns."
flowchart TD
  Q1{"Keep rows with<br/>no match?"}
  Q1 -->|"No"| INNER["inner_join"]
  Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"Unmatched from<br/>which side?"}
  Q2 -->|"Left x"| LEFT["left_join"]
  Q2 -->|"Right y"| RIGHT["right_join"]
  Q2 -->|"Both"| FULL["full_join"]
```

The question determines the join:

| Question | Join |
|---|---|
| Patients with both demographics and an outcome | `inner_join` |
| All patients, with their outcomes if any | `left_join`, demographics on the left |
| Patients with demographics but no outcome | `anti_join` |
| All patients from both files, even those in only one | `full_join` |

### Row counts on a toy example

The `dplyr` package ships two toy tables, `band_members` and
`band_instruments`, that make the row-count differences concrete.
Before you run the chunk, predict how many rows each join returns.

```{r}
#| label: joins-band
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

band_members
band_instruments

inner_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")  # John, Paul
left_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")   # + Mick (NA)
full_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")   # + Keith (NA)
anti_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")   # Mick only
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Write your predictions down as assertions. The chunk prints
nothing when every prediction holds, and stops at the first one
that does not.

```{r}
#| label: joins-band-verify
stopifnot(
  nrow(inner_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == 2,
  nrow(left_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) ==
    nrow(band_members),
  nrow(full_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == 4,
  nrow(anti_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")) == 1
)
```
:::

### Exercises

1. Use each of `inner_join`, `left_join`, `full_join`, and
   `anti_join` with the built-in `dplyr::band_members` and
   `dplyr::band_instruments` to produce four different tibbles.
   Write one sentence per result.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-15-1
#| message: false
inner_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")
left_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")
full_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")
anti_join(band_members, band_instruments, by = "name")
```

`inner_join` keeps only John and Paul, who appear in both.
`left_join` keeps all three band members, giving Mick an `NA`
instrument. `full_join` keeps Keith as well, giving him an `NA`
band. `anti_join` returns Mick alone: the band member with no
instrument row, and it adds no columns.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A collaborator asks for 'the patients in the
demographics file who have no outcome record'. Which join answers
this, and how many columns of the outcome table does the result
carry?

**Answer.** `anti_join(demographics, outcomes, by = "patient_id")`.
It is a filtering join, so it carries none of the outcome table's
columns: it returns rows of `demographics` only. A `left_join`
followed by `filter(is.na(outcome))` gives the same patients, but
it adds columns you then have to drop, and it misreads a patient
whose outcome record exists with a missing value as a patient with
no record.
:::

## Cardinality: when a join multiplies rows {#sec-joins-cardinality}

### Many-to-many joins

A many-to-many join occurs when both tables have duplicate keys:
each row in the left can match several rows in the right, and the
reverse. The result is the product of the matches for each key.

```{r}
#| label: joins-many-to-many
#| message: false
#| warning: true
library(dplyr)

a <- tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2), x = c("a", "b", "c"))
b <- tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2), y = c("p", "q", "r"))

# Five rows, not three: each id-1 in a joins each id-1 in b, giving
# four, plus the single id-2 match. dplyr warns because this is
# usually a key error rather than an intention.
inner_join(a, b, by = "id")
```

`dplyr` 1.1.0 and later warns by default. Take the warning
seriously: on a key that should be unique, it means rows have
multiplied. The fix is not to silence it but to declare the
relationship you expect:

```{r}
#| label: joins-relationship
#| error: true
# explicit; no warning, even with duplicates
inner_join(a, b, by = "id", relationship = "many-to-many")

# errors if duplicates exist on either side
inner_join(a, b, by = "id", relationship = "one-to-one")
```

### Declaring the relationship

The common case is many-to-one: several visits per patient, one
demographics row per patient. The three small tables below are
used by the rest of the chapter. P004 appears in `visits` but not
in `demographics`, a gap the audits in @sec-joins-keys are there
to catch.

```{r}
#| label: joins-fixtures
demographics <- tibble(
  patient_id = c("P001", "P002", "P003"),
  age        = c(64, 71, 52),
  sex        = c("F", "M", "F")
)
visits <- tibble(
  visit_id   = sprintf("V%02d", 1:6),
  patient_id = c("P001", "P001", "P002", "P002", "P003", "P004"),
  sbp        = c(148, 141, 155, 149, 132, 139)
)
labs <- tibble(
  visit_id  = c("V01", "V01", "V02", "V03"),
  test_code = c("HGB", "CRE", "HGB", "HGB"),
  value     = c(13.1, 0.9, 13.4, 11.8)
)

demographics
visits
labs
```

```{r}
#| label: joins-many-to-one
visits |>
  left_join(demographics, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "many-to-one")
# errors if a patient_id appears more than once in demographics
```

The assertion catches the data-quality bug at the join site,
where it is easiest to debug, instead of three scripts later as a
standard error that is too small.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A one-to-many join multiplies rows without a warning.** `dplyr`
warns only when keys repeat on *both* sides. If each visit key is
unique and a patient appears twice in `demographics` (a re-consent
appended rather than replaced), `left_join(visits, demographics)`
quietly returns an extra row for every visit of that patient. Only
`relationship = "many-to-one"` turns this into an error.
:::

### Exercises

2. Construct a scenario where an unintended many-to-many join
   duplicates rows. Write an assertion that catches the
   duplication before downstream analysis.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-15-2
#| error: true
#| warning: true
# demographics has a duplicated patient, perhaps from a
# re-consent that was appended rather than replaced
demo_dup <- tibble(patient_id = c("P001", "P001", "P002"),
                   age = c(64, 65, 71))
vis <- tibble(patient_id = c("P001", "P002"), sbp = c(148, 155))

# the silent version: two rows become three
left_join(vis, demo_dup, by = "patient_id")

# the assertion, before anything downstream runs
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(demo_dup$patient_id))
```

The join itself does not fail; it quietly returns more rows than
it received, and because `vis` has unique keys, `dplyr` does not
even warn. The `stopifnot()` fails loudly, which is the behavior
you want. Declaring `relationship = "many-to-one"` on the join
achieves the same thing at the point of use.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You join `visits` (10,000 rows) to `demographics`
(1,000 patients) on `patient_id`. The result has 12,500 rows.
What likely happened, and how do you find out?

**Answer.** The demographics table has duplicate `patient_id`
values, and each duplicate creates extra rows in the join output.
A clean many-to-one join returns 10,000 rows, one per visit; the
2,500 extra rows are the visits of patients with more than one
demographics record. Diagnose with:

```{r}
#| label: joins-key-duplicates
demographics |> count(patient_id) |> filter(n > 1)
```

Fix the duplication at its source. The tempting shortcut,
`distinct(patient_id, .keep_all = TRUE)`, keeps whichever row for
each patient happens to come first, so it chooses a record by file
order rather than by any rule: if the duplicates disagree on age
or sex, which one survives is an accident. If de-duplication is
right, state the rule in code (the most recent record, say, with
`slice_max()` on a date column). Adding
`relationship = "many-to-one"` to the join catches the problem at
the join site.
:::

## Keys and referential integrity {#sec-joins-keys}

A join that returns the number of rows you predicted usually did
what you meant; one that returns 'about the right number' is where
the bugs live. The checks below run before the analytic join and
take seconds.

### Auditing keys before the join

Two CRF (case report form) files that should cover the same
patients usually do not, exactly. `anti_join()` lists the patients
on one side that are absent from the other, which is the quickest
way to find missing records, ID typos, or a cohort mismatch.

```{r}
#| label: joins-key-audit
# uniqueness of keys
demographics |> distinct(patient_id) |> nrow()
demographics |> nrow()
# These should match for one-row-per-patient

# stopifnot for assertion
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(demographics$patient_id)))

# anti-join audit
visits |> anti_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |>
  distinct(patient_id)
# patients in visits with no demographics row
```

`assertthat` and `assertr` provide more elaborate assertions. For
most work, `stopifnot()` plus `anti_join()` audits cover the cases.

### Composite keys

When no single column identifies a row, name every column of the
key:

```{r}
#| label: joins-compound-key
reference_ranges <- tibble(
  test_code = c("HGB", "HGB", "CRE"),
  sex       = c("F", "M", "F"),
  age_group = c("50-70", "50-70", "50-70"),
  lower     = c(12.0, 13.5, 0.6),
  upper     = c(15.5, 17.5, 1.1)
)

labs |>
  left_join(visits, by = "visit_id") |>
  left_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |>
  mutate(age_group = "50-70") |>
  left_join(reference_ranges,
            by = c("test_code", "sex", "age_group"))
```

### Key types and representation

Document the canonical form of every identifier (character, with
leading zeros, upper case) and check it on every read. `dplyr`
refuses to join a character key to a numeric one, which is the
loud case. The quiet case is two character keys that spell the
same patient differently.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Lost leading zeros match nothing, and the row count does not
move.** If one file was read with `patient_id` as a number and
later converted with `as.character()`, `"001"` has become `"1"`.
A `left_join` on that key returns every row of the left table,
the count you expected, with `NA` in every right-hand column.
Read identifiers as character from the start
(`col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character())`).
:::

### Aside: updating a table by key with `rows_*`

The `rows_*` verbs update one table from another by key, and they
enforce key integrity as they go. They suit updating a master
patient list from a new extract.

```{r}
#| label: joins-rows-verbs
#| error: true
target <- tibble(id = 1:3, value = c("a", "b", NA))
source <- tibble(id = 3:4, value = c("c", "d"))

# insert new rows; error on key collision
rows_insert(target, source, by = "id")

# update existing rows; error if key not in target
rows_update(target, source, by = "id")

# upsert: insert new, update existing
rows_upsert(target, source, by = "id")

# patch: only update where target has NA; id 4 is not in target,
# so it must be ignored explicitly
rows_patch(target, source, by = "id", unmatched = "ignore")
```

`rows_upsert` adds new patients and updates existing ones;
`rows_patch` fills in missing values without overwriting existing
ones.

### Exercises

3. Use `rows_upsert` to merge two cohorts with overlapping
   patients (some new, some updated). Verify the result has the
   expected number of rows.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-15-4
cohort_1 <- tibble(patient_id = c("P001", "P002"),
                   status = c("enrolled", "enrolled"))
cohort_2 <- tibble(patient_id = c("P002", "P003"),
                   status = c("withdrawn", "enrolled"))

merged <- rows_upsert(cohort_1, cohort_2, by = "patient_id")
merged

# two originals plus one genuinely new patient
stopifnot(nrow(merged) == 3)
```

P002 is updated in place rather than duplicated, and P003 is
inserted. The row count is the check that distinguishes an upsert
from an accidental `bind_rows()`, which would have produced four
rows and two conflicting records for P002.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You `left_join` a 500-row visits table to a
demographics table and get 500 rows back, which is what you
expected. A colleague says this proves nothing. Are they right?

**Answer.** They are. A row count matching your expectation rules
out duplication and rules out nothing else. Every `patient_id` in
visits could have failed to match, and `left_join` would still
return exactly 500 rows, each with `NA` in every demographics
column. The lost-leading-zeros case above does exactly this.

Two checks catch it and the count does not. Count the `NA`s in a
column that came from the right-hand table, which should be zero
if every visit has demographics. And run the anti-join:

```r
visits |> anti_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |>
  distinct(patient_id)
```

An empty result means every key matched; a result listing every
patient means the join silently did nothing. `nrow()` is a
structural check, in the sense @sec-testing gives that term, and
structural checks pass on wrong answers.
:::

## Reshaping and stacking sources {#sec-joins-reshaping}

Some joins need wide data and others long; @sec-wrangling covers
`pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`. When several sources hold
alternative measurements of the same kind, the usual pattern is:

1. Convert each source to long format with consistent column names.
2. Stack the sources with `bind_rows()` rather than joining them.
3. Pivot wide for the modeling step.

For two CRF files from sites A and B with different column
conventions (display-only; the files are hypothetical):

```r
a_long <- read_csv("siteA.csv") |>
  clean_names() |>
  rename(bp_systolic = systolic_bp) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "measure")

b_long <- read_csv("siteB.csv") |>
  clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(matches("^(bp|sbp|dbp)_"), names_to = "measure")

combined <- bind_rows(a_long, b_long)
```

`bind_rows()` stacks; `bind_cols()` places tables side by side by
position, which is rarely correct for clinical data, because
nothing checks that row 12 of one table is the same patient as row
12 of the other. When the tables share a key, join on it.

### Exercises

4. Two wide tables represent patient visits at sites A and B with
   different column-name conventions. Reshape both to long and
   stack them so that downstream analysis treats them uniformly.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-15-3
#| message: false
library(tidyr)

site_a <- tibble(patient_id = "A01",
                 systolic_bp = 148, diastolic_bp = 88)
site_b <- tibble(patient_id = "B01",
                 sbp_1 = 155, dbp_1 = 91)

a_long <- site_a |>
  rename(bp_systolic = systolic_bp, bp_diastolic = diastolic_bp) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "measure")

b_long <- site_b |>
  rename(bp_systolic = sbp_1, bp_diastolic = dbp_1) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "measure")

bind_rows(a_long, b_long, .id = "site")
```

Renaming to a shared vocabulary *before* the pivot is what makes
`bind_rows()` safe. Stacking first and reconciling after leaves
you matching on strings that do not agree.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The long `labs` table has one row per visit and
test. You join it directly to `visits` on `visit_id`. What
relationship is that, and what happens to a later model that
expects one row per visit?

**Answer.** One-to-many: a visit with two tests appears twice.
Any per-visit model then counts that visit twice. Pivot `labs`
wide first, to one row per visit, and declare
`relationship = "one-to-one"` on the join; the worked example
below does both.
:::

## Worked example: a multi-source patient cohort {#sec-joins-worked}

The script below runs against the three fixture tables shown
earlier, written out as files so that it reads them as it would
read a real export. P004, who has visits but no demographics row,
is planted, so the audit warns once.

```{r}
#| label: joins-worked-example
#| message: false
#| warning: true
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

src <- file.path(tempdir(), "cohort")
dir.create(src, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(demographics, file.path(src, "demographics.csv"))
write_csv(visits, file.path(src, "visits.csv"))
write_csv(labs, file.path(src, "labs.csv"))

# read three sources
demographics <- read_csv(file.path(src, "demographics.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE) |> clean_names()
visits       <- read_csv(file.path(src, "visits.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE) |> clean_names()
labs         <- read_csv(file.path(src, "labs.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE) |> clean_names()

# labs is long, one row per visit and test, so its key is the pair
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(demographics$patient_id))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(visits$visit_id))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(labs[c("visit_id", "test_code")]))

# audit: patients in visits but no demographics
missing_demo <- visits |>
  anti_join(demographics, by = "patient_id") |>
  distinct(patient_id)

if (nrow(missing_demo) > 0) {
  warning("Patients in visits with no demographics: ",
          paste(missing_demo$patient_id, collapse = ", "))
}

# one row per visit, so that the lab join cannot add rows
labs_wide <- labs |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = test_code, values_from = value) |>
  clean_names()

# build the analytic dataset
analytic <- visits |>
  left_join(demographics, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "many-to-one", unmatched = "error") |>
  left_join(labs_wide, by = "visit_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(
    age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(0, 40, 65, Inf))
  )

# final row-count check: neither join may add or drop visits
stopifnot(nrow(analytic) == nrow(visits))

saveRDS(analytic, file.path(src, "analytic.rds"))
analytic
```

The script cleans names, verifies key uniqueness (on the composite
key for the long `labs` table), runs an `anti_join()` audit,
reshapes `labs` to one row per visit, performs the joins with
explicit `relationship` declarations, and asserts the final row
count. Joining the long `labs` table directly would have been
one-to-many and would have returned seven rows from six visits,
failing the final check. A reviewer can read the script and trust
the join semantics without re-deriving them.

`unmatched = "error"` is the companion to `relationship`.
`relationship` constrains how many rows each key matches;
`unmatched` constrains whether keys go unmatched at all. For a
left join it checks only the right-hand table, so here it stops
the script if a patient in `demographics` has no visits, while the
`anti_join()` audit covers the other direction.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the analytic dataset has one row per visit and that
the only visits without demographics are the ones the audit named.

```{r}
#| label: joins-worked-verify
stopifnot(
  nrow(analytic) == nrow(visits),
  !anyDuplicated(analytic$visit_id)
)
analytic |> filter(is.na(age)) |> distinct(patient_id)
```

The second line should list P004 and nobody else. Any other
patient here is a key that failed to match without an error.
:::

### The join checklist

Every join in the worked example passes the same seven checks,
collected in @tbl-join-checklist. They apply unchanged to joins
written in SQL (@sec-databases) and to the analysis datasets an
analysis plan specifies (@sec-analysis-plan).

| When | Check | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Before | The key is unique on the side that should have one row per key | `stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(x$key))` |
| Before | Key types and spelling agree (character, leading zeros, case) | `class(x$key)`; `head(sort(unique(x$key)))` |
| Before | Coverage in each direction | `anti_join(x, y, by = "key")` and `anti_join(y, x, by = "key")` |
| During | The relationship is declared | `relationship = "many-to-one"` |
| During | Unmatched keys are refused where none are allowed | `unmatched = "error"` |
| After | The row count is the one you predicted | `stopifnot(nrow(out) == nrow(x))` |
| After | Right-hand columns are not unexpectedly `NA` | `sum(is.na(out$col_from_y))` |

: The join checklist. Run it on every non-trivial join; the
first three rows take seconds and catch most join bugs before
they happen. {#tbl-join-checklist}

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An agentic version: a coding agent adds the assertions and runs
the script, and you review the evidence it reports rather than
only its code.

> **Context.** `R/build_analytic.R` joins `visits` (key
> `visit_id`; `patient_id` repeats) to `demographics` (one row per
> `patient_id`) and to `labs` (one row per `visit_id` and
> `test_code`). Column names and types are in
> `data/dictionary.csv`. Run the script only against the synthetic
> fixtures in `tests/fixtures/`.
>
> **Constraints.** Use `dplyr`. Add `relationship =` to every join,
> and `unmatched = "error"` wherever no key should go unmatched.
> Add a `stopifnot()` row-count check after each join. Do not
> change a join type, add `distinct()` or `filter()`, or declare
> `"many-to-many"` to make a check pass. Add no packages.
>
> **Criteria.** Before writing code, state the relationship you
> expect for each join and list your assumptions. After running,
> report for each join the row counts before and after and the
> anti-join audit in both directions. If any check fails, stop and
> report it instead of fixing it.

*Failure mode.* The agent silences a failing check by declaring
`"many-to-many"` or inserting `distinct()`, which hides the
duplicate the check found. *Check.* Search the diff for
`many-to-many`, `distinct(`, and new `filter(` calls; then run the
script yourself and walk @tbl-join-checklist. The agent sees the
dictionary, code, and synthetic rows, never patient data
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the worked example, why does the script pivot
`labs` wide *before* the join instead of after it?

**Answer.** Because the join to `visits` is meant to be
one-to-one. Pivoting first makes `visit_id` unique in `labs_wide`,
so `relationship = "one-to-one"` can be declared and the final
`nrow(analytic) == nrow(visits)` check can hold. Joining the long
table and pivoting afterward would multiply the visit rows in the
intermediate result, and any summary computed on that
intermediate would silently count some visits twice.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 6: count before and after every join.** Predict the row
   count, declare `relationship =` and, where it applies,
   `unmatched = "error"`, and let the code refuse anything else.
2. **Habit 8: a join that drops or multiplies rows produces a
   plausible number.** A matching row count is a structural check;
   pair it with an anti-join audit and an `NA` count on the
   right-hand columns.
3. **Habit 7: convert late, validate early.** Read identifiers as
   character, document their canonical form, and check it before
   the first join.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-teams).* Review a colleague's
   multi-table script (or one from a public analysis repository)
   for join safety alone. For every join, determine the intended
   relationship, check whether a `relationship` argument asserts
   it, and run an `anti_join()` audit on the keys. Report what you
   find as you would in a pull-request comment, naming the
   specific line and the specific risk, and use
   @tbl-join-checklist as your rubric.
6. *On your own work (no key).* Take a recent multi-table analysis
   of yours. Audit each join with `anti_join()` to identify
   missing keys, and document any unexpected gaps.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Keep matched rows only | `inner_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Unmatched rows (by dropping them) |
| Keep every row of `x` | `left_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Losing cohort members |
| Find rows of `x` with no match | `anti_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Silent gaps between files |
| Keep rows of `x` that match | `semi_join(x, y, by = "id")` | Adding columns you do not need |
| Assert the relationship | `relationship = "many-to-one"` | Row multiplication |
| Refuse unmatched `y` keys | `unmatched = "error"` | Silent non-matches |
| Find duplicated keys | `filter(count(x, id), n > 1)` | Duplicates before they join |
| Assert the row count | `stopifnot(nrow(out) == nrow(x))` | Rows added or dropped |
| Join on several columns | `by = c("test_code", "sex")` | Matching on a partial key |
| Update a table by key | `rows_upsert(x, y, by = "id")` | Duplicate records on update |
| Stack like sources | `bind_rows(a, b, .id = "site")` | Joining what should be stacked |

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-15}

1. `inner_join()` returns only rows whose key matches in both
   tables. `left_join()` returns every row from the left table;
   rows with no match on the right get `NA` in the right-hand
   columns. If the left table has 100 rows with keys A to J and
   the right table has only keys A to F, `inner_join` returns 60
   rows and `left_join` returns 100 rows (40 with `NA`s).
2. `anti_join(x, y)` returns rows of `x` whose key is *not*
   present in `y`. In a biomedical cleanup workflow it answers:
   'Which patients appear in my outcome file but not in the lab
   data?' (or the reverse). It thereby exposes missing data,
   duplicate IDs, or mismatched cohorts. Run it before the
   analytic join, so that problems surface early.
3. `table_a |> left_join(table_b, by = 'patient_id', relationship = 'many-to-one')`.
   A many-to-one join attaches the single table-B row to every
   table-A row sharing the key. The `relationship` argument errors
   if the relationship does not hold (for example, if `patient_id`
   is duplicated in table B).
